findings.claim: US Customs detained Uniqlo cotton shirts at Los Angeles in January 2021 under an order on Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps cotton, and in May 2021 rejected Uniqlo's protest, finding its evidence insufficient to show no forced labour was involved. Uniqlo cited cotton from Australia, Brazil and the US; CBP later took the rulings off its website, saying Uniqlo had withdrawn its protests.

NGOs and a Uyghur woman alleged in French complaints of 2021 and 2023 that Uniqlo and three other groups sold goods made partly with forced Uyghur labour; all four deny it. Prosecutors closed an initial inquiry, citing lack of jurisdiction, and a judge refused to open a judicial investigation, upheld on appeal in February 2025; a new complaint was announced.

About 2,000 workers lost jobs when Indonesian supplier Jaba Garmindo went bankrupt in 2015; Clean Clothes Campaign says they are owed $5.5 million in severance and that Fast Retailing refuses to contribute. An FLA investigation found no violation by Fast Retailing and suggested voluntary relief; the company funded an ILO project in Indonesia instead, and the FLA closed the case in October 2023.

Tokyo courts dismissed Fast Retailing and Uniqlo's ¥220 million defamation suit against publisher Bungeishunju in October 2013 and on appeal in March 2014, holding the important parts of its reporting on long hours in Japanese stores to be true. The Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal in December 2014, making the rulings final; they are over ten years old.

In October 2022 South Korea's Fair Trade Commission imposed a provisional fine of 153 million won on FRL Korea, Uniqlo's Korean operator, for overstating antibacterial and deodorising claims for AIRism and DRY-EX garments in ads run from 2018 to 2020.

By Fast Retailing's own figures, by FY2024 it had cut emissions from its stores and main offices by 83.3% and from its supply chain by 18.6% against FY2019, with 84.7% renewable electricity. The company raised its 2030 supply-chain target from 20% to 30% in November 2025.

Under agreements announced by Kyoto University in 2020, Yanai personally supports cancer immunology and iPS cell research there, including a commitment of ¥500 million a year from FY2021 to the iPS Cell Research Foundation. A clinical iPS cell production site named after him and funded from his gift opened in Osaka in June 2025.

social.reason: Documented company-level labour problems. US Customs blocked Uniqlo shirts in 2021, finding its evidence insufficient to show they were free of Xinjiang forced labour. A campaign says workers of a bankrupt Indonesian supplier are owed $5.5 million in severance; an FLA investigation found no violation by Fast Retailing. Japanese courts dismissed Uniqlo's defamation suit over reporting on long store hours, holding its key parts true (final 2014). French forced-labour complaints remain allegations.

legal.reason: Regulatory record at company level: a provisional fine of 153 million won on Uniqlo's Korean operator for misleading garment ads (2022) and the 2021 US customs detention of Uniqlo shirts. Fast Retailing also lost a defamation suit it brought over labour reporting (final 2014). No personal legal record for Tadashi Yanai was found.

unresolved.reason: No pending case or investigation was confirmed. Concerns raised by NGOs remain open: a campaign for unpaid severance at a former Indonesian supplier, to which Fast Retailing has declined to contribute, and forced-labour complaints in France that courts declined to investigate, with a new filing announced. Nothing personal is pending.

proposal.counterweights: Tadashi Yanai personally supports research at Kyoto University, including ¥500 million a year from FY2021 committed to its iPS cell foundation, whose site funded by his gift opened in 2025. Fast Retailing reports cutting supply-chain emissions 18.6% and its own 83.3% by FY2024 (its own figures).
proposal.rationale: Social stays 2, now documented: no forced-labour finding against Uniqlo itself (CBP found its evidence insufficient, not forced labour proven), so 3 is not supported. Legal 0 to 1: a Korean regulatory fine on a 51%-owned operator plus the CBP detention fit level 1. Unresolved 0 to 1: open NGO-raised concerns, but no pending case. Ecology and politics not proposed: the emissions disclosure is self-reported and no political activity was checked; ecology stays 3.
